subject: Chemistry
title: Amines and Diazonium Salts
summary: Amines are derivatives of ammonia: primary (RNH₂), secondary (R₂NH) and tertiary (R₃N). The nitrogen lone pair makes them bases and nucleophiles; nitrogen is sp³ and the molecule is pyramidal.

Aliphatic amines are stronger bases than ammonia (+I effect of alkyl groups); aromatic amines like aniline are much weaker (lone pair delocalised into the ring). In water the order is set by +I effect, solvation and steric hindrance together.
Primary, secondary and tertiary amines are told apart by the Hinsberg test, the carbylamine test (primary only) and their reactions with nitrous acid.
Aniline with NaNO₂/HCl at 0–5 °C gives benzenediazonium chloride, a versatile intermediate: Sandmeyer, Gattermann, coupling (azo dyes) and replacement by –OH, –I, –F, –H.

formulas.name: Reduction of nitro compounds
formulas.note: Fe/HCl is preferred: the FeCl₂ formed is hydrolysed, releasing HCl, so only a little acid is needed.

formulas.name: Gabriel phthalimide synthesis
formulas.formula: phthalimide + KOH → potassium phthalimide;  + RX → N-alkylphthalimide;  hydrolysis → RNH₂
formulas.mistake: Can't make aromatic amines (aryl halides don't undergo SN with phthalimide anion).

formulas.name: Hoffmann bromamide degradation
formulas.when: Amine with one carbon less than the amide.

formulas.name: Reduction of nitriles and amides
formulas.formula: RCN + LiAlH₄ (or H₂/Ni) → RCH₂NH₂ (one carbon more);  RCONH₂ + LiAlH₄ → RCH₂NH₂

formulas.name: Ammonolysis of alkyl halides
formulas.formula: RX + NH₃ → RNH₂ → R₂NH → R₃N → R₄N⁺X⁻
formulas.note: Gives a mixture; a large excess of NH₃ favours the primary amine.

formulas.name: Basicity in water (methyl)
formulas.note: In the gas phase the order is 3° > 2° > 1° > NH₃; in water solvation changes it.

formulas.name: Basicity of anilines
formulas.formula: p-toluidine > aniline > p-nitroaniline;  pKb larger = weaker base
formulas.note: Electron-donating groups increase basicity; −R/−I groups decrease it.

formulas.name: Hinsberg test
formulas.formula: C₆H₅SO₂Cl:  1° → sulphonamide soluble in KOH;  2° → sulphonamide insoluble in KOH;  3° → no reaction

formulas.name: Reaction with nitrous acid
formulas.formula: aliphatic 1° amine + HNO₂ → alcohol + N₂↑;  aniline + NaNO₂/HCl (273–278 K) → C₆H₅N₂⁺Cl⁻

formulas.name: Diazonium replacements
formulas.formula: CuCl/HCl → ArCl;  CuBr/HBr → ArBr;  CuCN/KCN → ArCN (Sandmeyer);  Cu/HX → ArX (Gattermann);  KI → ArI;  HBF₄, heat → ArF;  H₃PO₂ or ethanol → ArH;  warm water → ArOH

formulas.name: Coupling reaction
formulas.note: Here the N≡N group is retained — unlike replacement reactions.

examples.title: Hoffmann product
examples.problem: Propanamide is treated with Br₂ and NaOH. Product?
examples.solution: Ethanamine, CH₃CH₂NH₂ — one carbon less than the amide (CH₃CH₂CONH₂).

examples.title: Distinguish 1°, 2°, 3°
examples.problem: How do you tell ethylamine, diethylamine and triethylamine apart?
examples.solution: Hinsberg reagent: ethylamine gives a KOH-soluble sulphonamide; diethylamine gives an insoluble one; triethylamine does not react. Only ethylamine gives the carbylamine (foul smell) test.

examples.title: Why is aniline a weak base?
examples.problem: Explain why aniline is weaker than methylamine.
examples.solution: In aniline the lone pair on N is delocalised into the benzene ring (resonance), so it is less available for H⁺. In methylamine the +I effect of CH₃ makes the lone pair more available.

examples.title: Bromination of aniline
examples.problem: Aniline + bromine water? How to get only p-bromoaniline?
examples.solution: Bromine water gives 2,4,6-tribromoaniline (white ppt) because –NH₂ strongly activates the ring. Protect –NH₂ by acetylation (acetanilide), brominate (p-product), then hydrolyse.

examples.title: Nitration of aniline
examples.problem: Why does direct nitration of aniline give a large amount of m-nitroaniline?
examples.solution: In strongly acidic medium aniline is protonated to the anilinium ion (–NH₃⁺), which is meta-directing. About 47% meta product forms with para and some ortho, plus oxidation products.

examples.title: Diazonium route
examples.solution: Aniline + NaNO₂/HCl at 0–5 °C → benzenediazonium chloride; then CuCN/KCN (Sandmeyer) → C₆H₅CN.

topics.title: Structure and nomenclature
topics.explain: Nitrogen in amines is sp³ with a lone pair; C–N–C angle about 108°. Common names: methylamine, aniline (benzenamine), N,N-dimethylaniline. IUPAC: alkanamine (ethanamine), N-methylethanamine.

topics.title: Physical properties
topics.explain: Lower aliphatic amines are gases with a fishy smell. Primary and secondary amines form intermolecular hydrogen bonds; boiling points: 1° > 2° > 3° for isomeric amines. Tertiary amines have no N–H, so they cannot H-bond with each other.

topics.title: Acylation
topics.explain: Primary and secondary amines react with acid chlorides or anhydrides (nucleophilic substitution) to give amides; pyridine removes HCl. Benzoylation uses benzoyl chloride. Acetylation reduces the activating effect of –NH₂.

topics.title: Electrophilic substitution of aniline
topics.explain: –NH₂ is strongly activating and o/p-directing. Sulphonation gives sulphanilic acid, which exists as a zwitterion. Aniline does not undergo Friedel–Crafts reactions: it forms a salt with AlCl₃ (a Lewis acid), which deactivates the ring.

topics.title: Diazonium salts
topics.explain: ArN₂⁺X⁻; stable only at 273–278 K because the positive charge is delocalised over the benzene ring (aliphatic diazonium salts are unstable). They are used straight away in solution and are important for making aromatic compounds and dyes.

topics.title: Importance in daily life
topics.explain: Amines are found in proteins, vitamins, alkaloids and hormones; synthetic examples include drugs and dyes. Quaternary ammonium salts are used as detergents.

ratta: Hinsberg: 1° soluble in KOH, 2° insoluble, 3° no reaction.
Sandmeyer CuX;  Gattermann Cu/HX;  H₃PO₂ → ArH.
Aniline: no Friedel–Crafts; nitration gives ~47% meta.
